questions.prompt: In this course, why do virtually all major quantum computing SDKs (Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, Amazon Braket SDK) expose Python as their primary interface, even though the heaviest numerical computation happens elsewhere?
options: Python serves as an easy-to-read, fast-to-iterate control layer for describing and orchestrating circuits, while performance-critical linear algebra is handled by compiled libraries (like BLAS/LAPACK) that Python calls into
Python is the only programming language capable of representing complex numbers
Quantum hardware can only be controlled directly by Python code, with no compiled languages involved anywhere in the stack
Python was chosen arbitrarily and has no actual performance or ecosystem advantages for this purpose
questions.explain: The lesson's 'control layer vs. compute engine' split: Python owns describing what to run, while compiled BLAS/LAPACK code (called into via NumPy's @ operator) does the actual linear algebra.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson on setting up a scientific Python environment, which of the following are real benefits of using an isolated virtual environment (venv or conda) for this course's work?
options: Packages installed for this course won't silently conflict with or alter package versions needed by other, unrelated projects on the same machine
A requirements.txt file pinned to specific versions lets the exact same environment be recreated reproducibly on another machine
Virtual environments make NumPy's underlying BLAS/LAPACK computations run faster than they would in system Python
Once a virtual environment is created, it is impossible to ever install a different package version into it later
questions.explain: Isolation prevents cross-project package conflicts, and pinned requirements.txt files enable reproducible recreation elsewhere. Virtual environments have no effect on raw computation speed, and packages can always be added or changed later.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in NumPy, the operator used to perform real matrix multiplication (as opposed to element-wise multiplication with `*`) is the ____ operator.
questions.explain: NumPy overloads @ specifically for matrix multiplication (rows times columns), distinct from * which multiplies entries element-wise.

questions.prompt: You ran a notebook's cells out of page order (3, then 1, then 2) while exploring, and everything worked. A classmate opens the same notebook and selects 'Restart Kernel and Run All,' and it fails with a NameError. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A later cell (in page order) depends on a variable that was only defined because of the out-of-order execution sequence you used, and that variable no longer exists when cells run strictly top-to-bottom
The notebook file has become corrupted and must be deleted and rewritten from scratch
Restart Kernel and Run All is a broken Jupyter feature that should never be used
A NameError in a notebook always indicates a NumPy installation problem
questions.explain: Execution order in the kernel is not the same as page order; running cells out of sequence can hide a real dependency that only breaks when the notebook is run strictly top-to-bottom, which is exactly what Restart Kernel and Run All tests for.

questions.prompt: In the Qubit class example, apply_gate() returns a brand-new Qubit instance rather than modifying self.alpha/self.beta in place. What concrete debugging advantage does this give once five or six gates are chained in sequence?
options: Every intermediate Qubit object from each step can still be inspected afterward, making it possible to pinpoint exactly which gate application first produced an unexpected state
It makes the apply_gate method run noticeably faster than an in-place version
It is required because NumPy arrays cannot be modified in place under any circumstances
It prevents the class from ever needing a __repr__ method
questions.explain: The immutable-update pattern keeps every intermediate state around for inspection instead of overwriting the same variable repeatedly, which is exactly what makes a multi-gate chain debuggable.

questions.prompt: What is the key functional difference between the `*` operator and the `@` operator when applied to two 2D NumPy arrays representing matrices?
options: `*` multiplies corresponding entries element-wise (same shape required), while `@` performs real matrix multiplication (rows times columns, following linear-algebra shape rules)
`*` and `@` always produce identical results for any two matrices
`@` only works on 1D arrays, never on 2D matrices
`*` performs matrix multiplication while `@` performs element-wise multiplication
questions.explain: H * H just squares each entry of the Hadamard matrix, while H @ H computes the real matrix product and correctly gives the identity matrix, confirming H is its own inverse.

questions.prompt: Based on the Kronecker-products lesson, which of the following statements about np.kron are accurate?
options: np.kron(ket0, ket1) combines two 2-dimensional single-qubit vectors into one 4-dimensional two-qubit state vector
np.kron(X, I) and np.kron(I, X) produce the same 4x4 matrix, since matrix order doesn't matter in a Kronecker product
An n-qubit system built entirely from single-qubit pieces via repeated Kronecker products requires a 2^n-dimensional vector
The Kronecker product can only be applied to square matrices, never to vectors
questions.explain: kron(X,I) and kron(I,X) are confirmed to be different 4x4 matrices in the lesson (they flip different qubits), and np.kron works directly on vectors, not just square matrices -- both distractors are false.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: using the 2x2 eigenvalue formula (trace ± sqrt(trace^2 - 4*det)) / 2, the Pauli-Z matrix [[1,0],[0,-1]] has eigenvalues ____.
questions.explain: trace = 0, det = -1, giving eigenvalues (0 ± sqrt(4))/2 = +1 and -1, matching the two possible outcomes of a Z-basis measurement.

questions.prompt: CNOT was built in the Kronecker-products lesson as np.kron(P0, I) + np.kron(P1, X), where P0 and P1 are projectors onto the control qubit being |0> or |1>. When this CNOT matrix is applied to the state |10> (control=1, target=0), what happens and why?
options: The state becomes |11>, because the control qubit is |1>, which activates the np.kron(P1, X) term and flips the target qubit
The state remains |10>, because CNOT never changes any state
The state becomes |01>, because CNOT always swaps the two qubits
The state becomes |00>, because CNOT resets the target qubit to 0 whenever the control is 1
questions.explain: This was verified directly in the lesson: CNOT @ |10> = |11>, since the control being |1> triggers the X-on-target branch of the construction.

questions.prompt: Given G = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 1]]) and asked whether G could represent a valid quantum gate, what computation from the NumPy Linear Algebra Lab would you run, and what result would prove G is NOT valid?
options: Compute G @ G.conj().T and check with np.allclose against the identity matrix; since G's rows aren't orthonormal, the product will NOT be close to the identity, proving G is not unitary and therefore not a valid gate
Compute G + G.conj().T and check it equals zero; any nonzero result proves G is invalid
Check only whether G is a 2x2 matrix; since it is, G must already be a valid gate
Compute np.linalg.det(G) and confirm it is negative; a positive determinant would prove G is invalid
questions.explain: G @ G.conj().T evaluates to [[2,1],[1,1]], which is not the identity matrix, confirming G fails the unitarity test and so cannot represent a valid quantum gate.

questions.prompt: Based on the 'Complex Numbers in Python' lesson, which of these statements are accurate?
options: Python uses the suffix `j` (not `i`) to denote the imaginary unit, e.g. `4j`
The modulus (abs()) of a complex number z = a+bj equals sqrt(a**2 + b**2)
The conjugate of a complex number flips the sign of both its real and imaginary parts
cmath.polar converts a complex number from rectangular form to (modulus, angle) polar form
questions.explain: The conjugate only flips the sign of the imaginary part and leaves the real part unchanged, which makes option 3 (claiming both parts flip) false.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Python's built-in suffix for writing an imaginary number literal (e.g. in `4j`) is the letter ____.
questions.explain: Python always uses j as the imaginary unit suffix, never i (unlike standard math notation).

questions.prompt: The S-gate (phase gate), diag(1, j), was shown to be unitary but NOT Hermitian. What does this specific example prove about the relationship between the 'unitary' and 'Hermitian' properties of a matrix?
options: The two properties are independent -- a matrix can be a perfectly valid, probability-preserving quantum gate (unitary) without being equal to its own conjugate transpose (Hermitian)
Every unitary matrix must also be Hermitian, and the S-gate example was a special exception
A matrix cannot be unitary unless it is also Hermitian, so the S-gate is not actually a valid gate
Hermitian and unitary are two different names for exactly the same mathematical property
questions.explain: S @ S.conj().T is the identity (unitary), but S itself is not equal to S.conj().T (not Hermitian) -- direct proof the two properties don't imply each other.

questions.prompt: A teammate's code checks np.isclose(computed_norm, 1.0, atol=0.2) instead of NumPy's default atol=1e-8, and argues 'it still passes, so the code is fine.' Using the lesson's broken_total = 0.85 example, what real bug would this loosened tolerance fail to catch?
options: A genuinely broken computation producing a norm like 0.85 (off from 1.0 by 0.15) would incorrectly pass the check, even though this gap is far larger than ordinary floating-point rounding error (~1e-16)
It would fail to catch typos in variable names, which is unrelated to numeric tolerances
Loosening atol has no effect on which values pass or fail an np.isclose check
It would cause np.isclose to throw an exception instead of returning a boolean
questions.explain: The lesson's broken_total = 0.85 example is specifically chosen to show that a 0.15 discrepancy -- a real bug, not rounding noise -- would wrongly pass under an atol=0.2 tolerance that's far looser than the default.

questions.prompt: Based on the Complex Matrix Computation Lab's analysis of A = [[2, 1+1j], [1-1j, 3]], which statements are accurate?
options: A is Hermitian because its off-diagonal entries (1+1j and 1-1j) are complex conjugates of each other and its diagonal entries are real
A's eigenvalues, computed via the trace/determinant method, are exactly 1 and 4
np.linalg.eigvalsh(A) can return complex-valued eigenvalues for this matrix, since A itself contains complex entries
Every Hermitian matrix has entirely real eigenvalues, regardless of how many complex off-diagonal entries it contains
questions.explain: eigvalsh is specifically guaranteed to return real-dtype eigenvalues for a Hermitian matrix -- that's the whole point of using it over the general-purpose eigvals, making option 3 (claiming it can return complex values) false.

questions.prompt: Why does the 'Plotting Probability Distributions' lesson insist on bar charts rather than line plots for a qubit's measurement outcomes?
options: Quantum measurement outcomes are a fixed, discrete set of categories (e.g. 0 or 1) with no meaningful value 'between' them, so connecting them with a line would visually imply a relationship that doesn't exist
Matplotlib is technically incapable of drawing a line plot with only two data points
Bar charts always render faster than line plots in Matplotlib
Line plots cannot display a y-axis range between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Discrete, unconnected categories are exactly what a bar chart represents correctly; a line plot would falsely imply a continuous relationship between outcomes like 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: using x = sin(theta)*cos(phi), y = sin(theta)*sin(phi), z = cos(theta) with theta = pi/2 and phi = 0 (the |+> state), the Bloch-sphere coordinates (x, y, z) are ____.
questions.explain: sin(pi/2)*cos(0) = 1, sin(pi/2)*sin(0) = 0, cos(pi/2) = 0, landing the |+> state on the equator at (1, 0, 0), confirmed in the lesson's landmark-state table.

questions.prompt: According to the Bloch sphere lesson, which of the following are accurate?
options: theta controls the probability split between |0> and |1>, with |0> at the north pole and |1> at the south pole
phi controls a relative phase between the amplitudes that a plain probability bar chart cannot show at all
Two states with identical P(0) and P(1) values can still sit at different points on the Bloch sphere if their phi values differ
Every possible single-qubit state, regardless of theta and phi, sits at the exact center of the Bloch sphere
questions.explain: Pure single-qubit states sit on the SURFACE of the Bloch sphere, not at its center -- option 3 directly contradicts the lesson's description of the Bloch sphere as a unit sphere whose surface points represent pure states.

questions.prompt: For a state with P(0)=0.25, P(1)=0.75, simulated for N=1000 shots, the lesson computes 'expected counts' of 250 and 750. Why does the lesson emphasize these are the EXPECTED counts rather than guaranteed exact results of any one real run?
options: The expected counts (N x probability) describe the long-run average outcome; any single real run is subject to statistical noise and might report, for example, 243 and 757 instead, purely by chance
Because 250 and 750 are actually wrong, and a real run would always report exactly 500 and 500
Because expected counts only apply when N is less than 100
Because probabilities and counts are unrelated quantities with no mathematical connection
questions.explain: N * probability is exact, deterministic arithmetic describing the theoretical average; it is explicitly not a promise about any one simulated run, which is subject to statistical noise.

questions.prompt: Per the Matplotlib Fundamentals lesson, what does the label= keyword argument on a .plot() call actually do, and what happens if it's omitted on one series in a multi-series plot?
options: label= feeds ax.legend() so that series gets an entry; if omitted, that series still draws on the plot but does NOT appear in the legend
label= changes the color of the line automatically based on the text provided
Omitting label= on any series causes Matplotlib to throw a runtime error immediately
label= is required for a line to be drawn on the Axes at all
questions.explain: The lesson states label= on each .plot() call feeds ax.legend(); without a label, a series still shows up in the plot but not in the legend.

questions.prompt: A labmate says their quantum circuit simulation gives a different measurement histogram every time they run it, making it impossible to tell if a circuit change actually did anything. Per the Random Seeds lesson, what single change fixes this, and why does it work?
options: Use a seeded generator (e.g. np.random.default_rng(42)) for the sampling step; the same seed deterministically reproduces the exact same sequence of 'random' draws every run, isolating the effect of any code change
Switch from NumPy to plain Python's random module, which never uses pseudo-randomness
Increase the number of shots to one million, which eliminates all randomness
Remove all randomness from the simulation entirely, since quantum measurement sampling should never involve randomness
questions.explain: A PRNG is deterministic given a fixed seed -- seeding the generator makes repeated runs produce identical sampled output, which is exactly the reproducibility guarantee the lesson establishes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the modern, recommended NumPy function for creating a seeded random number generator instance (as opposed to the legacy global-state np.random.seed) is ____.
questions.explain: np.random.default_rng(seed) returns an explicit generator instance, avoiding the hidden global state that the legacy np.random.seed approach relies on.

questions.prompt: Per the 'Documenting Numerical Results Honestly' lesson, which of the following should accompany a reported numerical result (like a simulated fidelity) for it to be considered reproducible?
options: The random seed used, if the result depended on sampling
The exact computation performed (e.g. which formula or function produced the number)
The comparison tolerance used, if the result involved a floating-point equality check
The exact make and model of the computer the code ran on
questions.explain: The lesson's reproducibility checklist is seed, computation, and tolerance -- hardware model is never listed as a required element.

questions.prompt: A specific published result ('Bell state fidelity = 0.9987') depends on one exact state of the code. Per the Version Control lesson, what should you do so that exact code state can always be found again, even after dozens of later commits change the main branch?
options: Create an annotated git tag (e.g. v1.0-bell-fidelity-result) on that exact commit, so git checkout <tag> can always reconstruct that precise code state later
Rename the file to include the number 0.9987 in its filename
Delete the branch immediately after the result is published, so it can never be changed
Write the result only in a code comment, since comments are permanently frozen once committed
questions.explain: A git tag permanently marks one specific commit, letting git checkout reliably reconstruct that exact code state regardless of how far main has since moved.

questions.prompt: A raw computed value of 0.99872345 is reported two different ways elsewhere in a project: 'fidelity = 0.9987' (rounded to 4 decimal places) and 'fidelity = 0.999' (rounded to 3 significant figures). Per the Documenting Numerical Results Honestly lesson, when do these two different-looking roundings become dishonest?
options: Only if the rounding method isn't stated, or if either rounded number is presented as a separate, more precise measurement rather than a rounding of the same underlying value
They are always dishonest, since a result must only ever be reported with full floating-point precision
Only the 4-decimal-place rounding is ever acceptable in scientific work
They are never dishonest under any circumstances, regardless of what is stated alongside them
questions.explain: Rounding for readability is fine when labeled as rounding; it becomes dishonest only when the rounding method is hidden or the result is implied to be more precise than it actually is.

questions.prompt: A classmate wants to add support for arbitrary n-qubit systems and a full noise model to their capstone before building the basic 2-qubit Bell-state case. Per the Capstone Kickoff lesson's scoping argument, what should they build first instead, and why?
options: The small, correctly-working 1-2 qubit case first -- the same core skills (state representation, gate application, probability math) apply at any scale, so finishing a small correct version first minimizes implementation risk compared to attempting a larger scope immediately
The noise model first, since noise is more important than correctness
Nothing -- arbitrary n-qubit support and noise modeling should always be attempted before any smaller working version exists
A circuit-drawing visualization tool, since that was the lesson's primary recommended first step
questions.explain: The lesson's scope-discipline argument: a correct small version exercises the same underlying skills as a larger one, at far less implementation risk, and is the recommended starting point.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per the capstone build lessons, calling probabilities() on the Bell state [0.707107, 0, 0, 0.707107] should return ____.
questions.explain: 0.707107 squared rounds to 0.5, and the zero amplitudes square to exactly 0, giving the Bell state's confirmed 50/50 split between |00> and |11>.

questions.prompt: The Capstone Wrap-Up & Code Review lesson lists specific, independently-verifiable facts a reviewer should check the toolkit's code against. Which of these are among those listed facts?
options: apply_gates([kron_gate(H, I), CNOT], zero_state(2)) must equal [0.707107, 0, 0, 0.707107]
probabilities(bell_state) must equal [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5], never with nonzero probability on |01> or |10>
bloch_coordinates([1/sqrt(2), 1/sqrt(2)]) must equal (1, 0, 0) within floating-point tolerance
The toolkit's plotting functions must render in under 10 milliseconds on every machine
questions.explain: The lesson lists exactly three known-fact correctness checks (Bell-state construction, Bell-state probabilities, and |+> state Bloch coordinates); a plotting-speed requirement was never part of the review checklist.

questions.prompt: Your probabilities() function, run on a state you believe is the Bell state, returns [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] instead of [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5]. Per the Capstone Measurement & Visualization lesson, what does this specific wrong pattern most strongly suggest?
options: The two qubits likely never became entangled -- an equal 25% spread across all four basis states is the signature of two independent, uncorrelated superpositions, suggesting CNOT was never correctly applied
The probabilities() function itself must be broken, since it should always return [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5] regardless of input
This output is actually correct, and the lesson's claimed [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5] result was wrong
This pattern provides no useful information about where a bug might be
questions.explain: Equal probability across all four basis states is exactly what two independent, uncorrelated 50/50 superpositions would produce -- pointing back at the gate-application (CNOT) step rather than the probability function.

questions.prompt: The Capstone Wrap-Up lesson names specific test-coverage gaps (no test for invalid/non-normalized input, no single-qubit-only test, no empty-gate-list test) even though the existing three tests pass. Why does the lesson treat naming these gaps as important rather than a minor afterthought?
options: Honestly naming what is NOT tested, rather than treating the tests that happen to exist as full coverage, applies Chapter 5's documentation-honesty discipline to testing instead of numerical results
Because any codebase with an untested edge case should be deleted and rewritten from scratch
Because Python's testing framework refuses to run any tests until 100% coverage is reached
Because the three existing tests are actually written incorrectly and must be discarded
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this to Chapter 5's honesty theme: naming untested gaps, rather than implying the existing tests are complete coverage, is the honest practice being modeled.
